chapter.title: Face in, breath out

cards.body:
Hold your breath right now and count to 10. Feel your shoulders creep up toward your ears? That is what most beginners do the second their face touches water, and it is why the water feels like it is fighting them.

The water is a bed you lie on. You can't rest on a bed with clenched fists. **Breathing out into the water is how you unclench.**
cards.simpler: Hold your breath and count to 10. Notice your shoulders rising toward your ears? That is what most beginners do the moment their face touches water. It is why the water feels like it is fighting them. Think of the water as a bed you lie on. You can't rest on a bed with clenched fists. **Breathing out into the water is how you unclench.**

cards.prompt: Priya puts her face in a warm pool, lips sealed tight. Two seconds later her chest is screaming and she bursts up, gasping. What most likely went wrong?

options.text: She held her breath with her mouth shut, so her body sounded the alarm fast.
The pool was too cold and her body reacted to the temperature.
She forgot to pinch her nose, so water got in.

whyNot.b: That's a shiver, not a scream: the pool was warm, and a held breath feels urgent within seconds whatever the temperature.
whyNot.c: That's the old habit, not the fix: air going out of your nose keeps water out, so pinching isn't needed and isn't what caused the panic.

cards.reteach: A held breath behind a closed mouth builds pressure, and the urge to breathe arrives in a few seconds however fit you are. Letting air trickle out slowly removes that pressure. The water didn't attack Priya. Her closed mouth did.

cards.title: Hum it out
cards.body:
Stand in chest-deep water, both hands on the wall. Lower your face until your ears are nearly in. Now hum. A slow, steady hum sends a thin stream of air out through your nose and mouth, and you'll see it as *bubbles*, the little proof that you're breathing out and not holding.

Air leaving your nose is also a door closing. **While air is going out, water can't come in**, which is why you don't need to pinch anything.

Keep your eyes open. The pool is blurry and greenish and completely fine. Three seconds of humming, then lift.
cards.simpler: Stand in chest-deep water, both hands on the wall. Lower your face until your ears are almost under. Now hum. A slow, steady hum pushes a thin stream of air out through your nose and mouth. You will see bubbles. They prove you are breathing out, not holding. **While air is going out, water can't come in**, so you don't need to pinch your nose. Keep your eyes open. The blurry green view is fine. Three seconds, then lift.

cards.title: Marcus and the birthday song
cards.body: Marcus, first lesson, ducks his face in like he's bobbing for apples: lips sealed, cheeks full. He's up in 2 seconds, gasping, both hands wiping his eyes. The teacher asks him to hum Happy Birthday into the water instead. He gets as far as "dear Mar-" before he needs air, which is a good 4 seconds, and comes up calm, eyes open, hands still on the wall. He looks faintly offended that it worked.
cards.simpler: Marcus is in his first lesson. He dips his face in like he is bobbing for apples: lips sealed, cheeks full. He pops up after 2 seconds, gasping, both hands wiping his eyes. The teacher asks him to hum Happy Birthday into the water instead. He gets as far as "dear Mar-" before needing air. That is a good 4 seconds. **He comes up calm**, eyes open, hands still on the wall. He looks almost offended that it worked.

cards.prompt: You're at the wall in chest-deep water, about to practise. Which version is the one this chapter teaches?

options.text: Face in, lips sealed, count to 5 in your head, pop up and take a big gulp of air.
Face in, hum a steady stream of bubbles for 3 seconds, lift your chin just clear of the water, breathe in through your mouth, face back in.
Face in, blast all your air out in one hard puff, then lift and breathe in.

whyNot.a: That's holding, not breathing out: sealed lips are what made Priya's chest scream.
whyNot.c: That's a dump, not a stream: one hard puff empties you in a second, so you come up gasping instead of calm.

cards.reteach: Think of blowing on hot soup: slow, steady, under control. That's the out-breath, and it lasts about 3 seconds. The in-breath is a quick open mouth just above the surface, then straight back down.

cards.title: The quick part
cards.body:
You'd think the in-breath is the hard part. It's the easy part. Once you've hummed air out for 3 seconds, lift your chin until your mouth just clears the surface, open it, and air falls in on its own. No gulp needed. Then face back in and hum again.

So the rhythm is long out, short in. About 3 seconds out, 1 second in, a slow kettle rather than a sprinter.

**Hands stay where they are.** No wiping eyes, no pinching nose. Goggles are fine if you like them. The wipe is the habit to drop, because it drags your head out of the rhythm every single time.
cards.simpler: Breathing in is the easy part. After you hum air out for 3 seconds, lift your chin until your mouth just clears the water. Open it, and air falls in by itself. Long out, short in: about 3 seconds out, 1 second in, a slow kettle rather than a sprinter. **Hands stay where they are.** No wiping eyes, no pinching nose. Goggles are fine. Drop the wipe. It pulls your head out of the rhythm every time.

cards.body: Dana gets ready to go under like a free diver: huge breath in, cheeks puffed like a trumpet player, shoulders up. She lasts 6 seconds, which feels like a win, then surfaces gasping and needs a rest before the next go. Spot it by the puffed cheeks and the gasp. The fix is smaller, not bigger: a normal breath, then a slow hum out.
cards.simpler: Dana gets ready to go under like a diver about to go deep: a huge breath in, cheeks puffed like a trumpet player, shoulders up. She lasts 6 seconds, which feels like a win. Then she comes up gasping and needs a rest before trying again. You can spot this by the puffed cheeks and the gasp. **The fix is smaller, not bigger.** Take a normal breath, then hum out slowly.

cards.prompt: You're watching a friend practise from the side of the pool. Which sign tells you they're holding their breath instead of breathing out?

options.text: A steady line of small bubbles coming up past their ears.
Puffed cheeks underwater, then a gasp when they surface.

whyNot.a: That's the goal, not the problem: bubbles are the proof air is leaving.
whyNot.c: That's the eyes, not the breath: open eyes are exactly what you want, and tell you nothing about air.

cards.reteach: Held air has to go somewhere, so it shows in the cheeks and comes out as a gasp. Breathing out shows as bubbles and ends with a calm, small in-breath. Watch the surface, not the swimmer's face: bubbles mean they're doing it.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Face in, eyes open, hum a slow stream of bubbles out through nose and mouth for about 3 seconds, then lift your chin just enough to let air fall back in. The water isn't something you hold your breath against; it's where the out-breath goes.

Tomorrow: can you stand up from a back float? Most beginners freeze there.
cards.simpler: Face in, eyes open. Hum a slow stream of bubbles out through your nose and mouth for about 3 seconds. Then lift your chin just enough to let air fall back in. **The water is not something you hold your breath against.** It is where your out-breath goes. Tomorrow: can you stand up from a back float? Most beginners freeze there.

cards.body: Tonight, fill the bathroom sink with warm water. Face in, eyes open, hum for 3 seconds, lift, breathe in. Do it 10 times. Towel stays on the rail until you're done.
cards.simpler: Tonight, fill the bathroom sink with warm water. Put your face in with your eyes open. Hum for 3 seconds, then lift and breathe in. Do this 10 times in a row. **The towel stays on the rail** until all 10 are done. No wiping between goes.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now put your face in the water 10 times in a row, breathing out slowly each time and in above the surface, without wiping your eyes or pinching your nose.
